title: Steak and ale pie
subtitle: tender braised beef in ale under a golden shortcrust lid
excerpt: Steak and ale pie is a braised beef filling under a shortcrust pastry lid, baked until the top is golden and firm. The ale gives the gravy depth and a slight bitterness that balances the richness of the beef. Watch the sauce level before topping: it should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, or the lid will sink as it bakes.
sourceNotes: Steak and ale pie is a standard of British pub and home cooking, documented across 20th-century household cookery. The shortcrust lid-only construction (rather than a double crust) is the more common home format, giving a thicker filling-to-pastry ratio. The method follows the braised-then-topped pattern used across British farmhouse cookery references.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the filling separately for up to 3 months. Make fresh pastry to top.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. Top with pastry and bake on the day.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. Middle to upper shelf. The pie lid needs direct top heat to colour and crisp.

glossaryTerms.definition: A method of cooking meat slowly in a small amount of liquid, covered, at a low temperature. The meat starts by browning in hot fat to develop colour and flavour, then finishes in the covered pot where steam and liquid break down tough connective tissue into tender, silky strands.

A pastry made by rubbing cold fat into flour until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs, then binding with the minimum amount of cold water. The fat coats the flour particles and limits gluten development, giving a crumbly, tender result rather than a chewy one.

Leaving cooked meat or a baked dish to sit before cutting or serving. In a pie, resting for 10 minutes after the oven allows the filling to firm slightly so it does not pour out when the crust is broken.

content.text: Steak and ale pie is a
braised
beef filling cooked low and slow in ale, then topped with
shortcrust pastry

and baked. The filling and pastry are made separately, so you can braise the beef up to two days ahead and top the pie on the day. The key risk is a filling that is too liquid when you lid the pie: reduce it properly before it goes into the dish, or the pastry will be wet and heavy rather than golden and crisp.
Method
Braising the filling
Pat the beef chunks dry and season generously with salt and pepper. Dust with the 2 tablespoons of plain flour and toss to coat.
Heat the sunflower oil in a large saucepan or casserole over high heat. Brown the beef in batches, leaving space between pieces so they colour rather than steam. Remove each batch and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onions and carrots to the same pan and cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

Stir in the tomato puree and cook for 1 minute. Return the browned beef to the pan. Pour in the ale and beef stock. Add the thyme sprigs and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then cover and cook on a very low heat for 2 to 2 hours 30 minutes until the beef is tender and pulls apart easily.

Remove the thyme and bay leaves. If the sauce is loose, remove the lid and simmer uncovered for 10 to 15 minutes until it coats the back of a spoon. Taste and season. Transfer to the pie dish and leave to cool completely before topping.
Making the shortcrust lid

Put the 300 g plain flour, 1 teaspoon salt, and 150 g cold cubed butter into a bowl. Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture looks like rough breadcrumbs with no large butter pieces remaining.
Add the cold water a tablespoon at a time, cutting through with a knife, until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork it. Press into a disc, wrap in cling film, and chill for 30 minutes.
Topping and baking
Preheat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius conventional. Roll the chilled pastry on a lightly floured surface to a shape slightly larger than your pie dish.

Brush the rim of the pie dish with beaten egg. Lay the pastry over the cold filling and press gently onto the rim to seal. Trim the overhang. Cut two small slits in the centre to let steam escape. Brush the surface all over with beaten egg.

Bake for 28 to 32 minutes until the pastry is deep golden and firm to the touch at the centre. A skewer pushed through a slit should feel hot when held against your wrist. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

attrs.heading: If something went wrong
attrs.intro: The four most common problems with a steak and ale pie, and what to do about them.

items.symptom: Pastry is soggy and pale on the underside of the crust
items.cause: Filling was too liquid or too warm when the lid went on.
items.fix: Reduce the filling to a thick gravy before it goes into the dish. The filling must be completely cold before you top it.
items.avoid: Avoid lidding a pie with a filling that moves freely when you tilt the dish.

items.symptom: Pastry lid sinks into the filling
items.cause: The filling shrank during baking and pulled the pastry down.
items.fix: Fill the pie dish right to the top before adding the lid. A pie funnel in the centre also helps.
items.avoid: Avoid leaving a gap of more than 1 cm between the filling surface and the pastry.

items.cause: Not braised long enough, or heat was too high.
items.fix: Test a piece after 2 hours: it should give with gentle pressure. If it resists, give it another 20 to 30 minutes covered.
items.avoid: Avoid a rapid boil during braising; the liquid should barely tremble.

items.symptom: Pastry cracks and does not hold together when cut
items.cause: Pastry was overworked or too much water was added.
items.fix: Work the dough only until it comes together. Add water one tablespoon at a time and stop as soon as the dough holds.
items.avoid: Avoid pressing or kneading the dough once it has formed.

attrs.title: Which ale to use
attrs.body: A dark ale or bitter gives the best depth of flavour. Avoid very hoppy IPAs, which can make the sauce bitter over a long braise. A standard 500 ml can of brown ale or a traditional English bitter works well.

content.text: After
resting
the pie for 10 minutes, the filling will be thick enough to serve in clean spoonfuls rather than flooding the plate.
